speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this morning to speak to the motion of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice concerning an Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne-although my speaking time has unfortunately been cut somewhat-because although a Throne Speech is not detailed in the same way that a Budget speech is, in

May 27, 1991
The Address
this case, mentions, essentially, the major challenges facing us and proposes ways of meeting those challenges.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the Throne deals first of all with Canadian unity, and the challenge to Canadians to choose the kind of Canada we want. When we talk about unity, we cannot isolate unity from economic prosperity, and I will get back to this later on in my speech. And when we talk about prosperity, if we are at all serious about what we are saying, we must necessarily mention education, because here again, we have a major problem where the Goverment of Canada must show leadership in providing the necessary solutions. And speaking of challenges, when we think back to last summer's native crisis, I think that here again the Speech from the Throne provides some very concrete solutions. The same applies to our economic problems; to that cornerstone of our Canadian values, the family; and also to one particular group in our society where this government has provided a number of solutions to enable the disabled to play a more active role. The same applies when we talk about government responsiveness, about making members better able to represent their constituents, and about this government's commitment to cutting government spending and reducing the debt.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to the first subject, Canadian unity. In the Speech from the Throne, we see that the government has promised to appoint a committee by next September that will consult with legislative assemblies, in other words with the various provincial members, and with Canadians in general. There is an important element here, the government will formulate proposals, to be referred to the committee. There has been a lot of criticism and there have been many suggestions about how to deal with this problem, how to meet this challenge and how to provide solutions, but the fact remains that this is not one more exercise in consultation. We must not forget that this committee will have concrete proposals to discuss, and in the present unity debate, we see that the Goverment of Quebec, for instance, has also appointed a committee that will apparently receive Ottawa's proposals.
Mr. Speaker, receiving the proposals is fine, but in the light of our past experience-and this is where Quebec adds an important dimension-proposals submitted by Canada should first be ratified by what is called English Canada. This is where the committee plays an extremely important role, because, once again, it will have concrete proposals from this government.
The committee will then consult English Canada in particular to be able to come to Quebec so that we can finally find a solution.
Mr. Speaker, I looked at the comments of the media and the general public on that aspect of the Speech from the Throne. One need only put forward a solution to hear all sorts of criticisms; everyone has his own solution. What I found unfortunate in all those criticisms is the negativism. For example, the Meech Lake Accord is always spoken of as a failure. If we want to be objective and see things differently, we could say that Meech Lake nearly succeeded.
Mr. Speaker, you know that in this wonderful country, Canada, it is not for nothing that the first ministers have spent a great deal of time discussing the amending formula at federal-provincial conferences since 1965. Everyone seemed to agree that unanimity was practically impossible; so much so, Mr. Speaker, that when the Constitution was repatriated in 1982, Mr. Trudeau, who was then Prime Minister of Canada, also tried to obtain the unanimity rule, but seeing how difficult it was, he forcibly repatriated the Constitution without Quebec's agreement. He understood so well that unanimity was impossible that he later inserted this famous unanimity rule at the time of repatriation so that when we had what is now called the Meech Lake Accord, Prime Minister Mulroney had to use the laws, regulation and rules imposed at repatriation, namely the three-year deadline for the various provincial legislatures to ratify the accord unanimously-that is, all ten provinces and the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I said Meech Lake was practically a success because, as you will recall, within the process imposed by the previous government, this government was able to obtain the unanimous consent of the provinces on two occasions: the first time in 1987, at what I will call the beginning of this debate, when all First Ministers, including the Prime Minister of Canada,
May 27, 1991

ratified the accord; and a second time on June 9, 1990, when the 11 First Ministers of this country again ratified the Meech Lake Accord.
So Meech Lake was not really a failure. It was almost a success. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that with this new experiment, this new committee and this new department, if each and everyone of us takes a positive and constructive attitude instead wanting to tear the country apart, I am sure we will meet the challenge that Canadian unity represents.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time has almost expired. I will therefore conclude my remarks on the economic aspects, and more specifically on education, a subject that has aroused some very fierce criticism in connection with provincial jurisdiction. In this country, from Vancouver to Halifax, we have an illiteracy rate of 30 per cent, which means people who do not know how to read or write. Forty per cent of our young people do not finish high school. I think someone has to take the lead, but I repeat, although the government announced that it would intervene in this field, it also said that it would do so without encroaching on provincial jurisdictions.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about unity and the Constitution, we cannot overlook the aspect of our economy, and especially our young people who are the future of this country.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne rightfully linked the two concepts of national unity and economic prosperity.
They certainly go hand in hand. In fact, they support each other. We all agree, as a country, that we must be competitive in order to maintain our standard of living.
We tend to forget what a large percentage of our Gross Domestic Product is dependent on foreign trade. This percentage is even more than that of the United States and Japan. We have to be cognizant of this fact when we consider economic policies for the country.
There has been a great deal of change and restructuring of our economy as we move to meet the goal of making our economy more competitive. We would all like this change to be calm and rational, however that is not always the case.
The Address
We cannot be reactionary and think that we are going to rely simply on a market of 26 million people for goods and services. That is unrealistic in the world today.
First, we must break down the trade barriers that exist within our own country between the provinces. We have to develop a free market within our own country. This is one of the goals of the throne speech that I certainly endorse.
In order for Canadians to be competitive we are going to need a great deal of co-operation among governments, business, labour and everyone else in the country. This is one aspect of the budget speech from the province of Ontario that I would certainly endorse, although I cannot support the large deficit financing associated with that budget.
That type of thinking in the past is one of the reasons that the federal government finds itself in its current position with very little room to manoeuvre.
The issue of competitiveness is one that is foremost in my community of St. Catharines at the present time. We see the spectre of cross-border shopping, which is affecting the retail industry as well as other areas of the local economy. People certainly have the right to get the best value for their money wherever they can, as long as they abide by the rules and pay the various duties and taxes on these goods.
The answer to this matter is not to close down the border, as some people have suggested, but to make sure that our industry is competitive. This requires all levels of government to review their taxation and regulation policies, and business to look at its own practices in order to ensure that it is competitive. Governments at the municipal, provincial and federal levels have to review their policies and do everything they can to ensure that our industries are competitive.
This is a complex matter. It is not a simple matter. People would say there is a simple solution to it, but as with most things these days, that is not the case. We all have to look at the problem, all deal with it, and all accept ownership of it.
The automobile parts industry is also important to my area. This is an industry that is also in a very tough, competitive position. Again, governments at all levels must review their policies to ensure they are not penaliz-

May 27, 1991
The Address
ing these industries. The industiy has to review its practices in order to ensure that it is using technologically advanced processes and that it is creating high quality value added parts. It has to use new technologies in order to compete. Labour also has to do its part to ensure that these industries are competitive.
Economic prosperity will allow us to deal with the matter of national unity. I have had the opportunity, as a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, to travel across Canada listening to individual Canadians speak about the Constitution and the amending formula. The committee is currently considering the recommendations we received from across the country regarding the amending formula. Therefore, I will not comment on that particular aspect of the matter.
However, the committee heard many of the goals and aspirations of the various regions and groups in the country. I agree with those individuals who have stated that this round of constitutional negotiations must be the Canada round. It is going to take a great deal of compromise, tolerance and understanding. It is something that we have to begin.
The aboriginal people want the concept of self-government to be discussed constitutionally. There may be some difficulty because the definition they attach to that concept varies across the country. As we negotiate land claims that concept is included in some of the settlements. As I mentioned, it means different things to different bands in different parts of the country. That is going to create some difficulty in trying to entrench that concept constitutionally.
The aboriginal people also mentioned the concept of consent regarding any constitutional change affecting them. We will have to try and deal with this matter and realize that the concept of consent is very similar to the concept of veto. We have heard about this concept in other contexts in conjunction with the Constitution.
The various aboriginal groups feel they can define exactly what is meant by protecting their language and their culture. Although, as we have seen, it even affects our institutions and maybe affects the entire Constitution itself. We have to try and deal with this matter. Again, it is a complex matter, something that is not very simple.
We heard from the people of the north that they would like a return to the pre-1982 state of affairs regarding the creation of provinces, in which the individual territories negotiated with the federal government in creating new provinces. We also heard of the discontent of the people of the north with the current provision in the Constitution about the extension of current provinces into the territories and the method by which that could occur. They feel slighted by that. They want that matter addressed in the current round. That is something we will have to deal with as well.
We heard from minority language groups in the various regions of the country. They have expressed a strong desire for their language and rights to be protected. As always, we have to be cognizant of their interests as well. We have to realize that there are one million francophones outside Quebec, and the need for the rights of the anglophone minority in the province of Quebec to continue to be protected.
Quebec feels that the rules of the game have been changed on it in the last 30 years by various means. It has expressed this in the Belanger-Campeau report and the Allaire report. We want Quebec to be part of the constitutional process, and it is necessary that we deal with this matter. We cannot emasculate the federal government but we must give recognition to the need for Quebec to protect its language, culture and uniqueness within the Canadian mosaic. It was well set out within the throne speech and it is a matter that we are obviously going to have to deal with.
The people of the west and some in the Atlantic region desire an institutional means in order to recognize the regional diversity of the country. There has been a great deal of energy put into the concept of a Triple E Senate in order to recognize this diversity. I have some hesitancy in saying that this would actually solve all their concerns in this regard.
We heard an expert from Australia who mentioned the Australian Senate which was set up with equal numbers of senators from each of the states within the country of Australia in order to try and resolve these regional differences. It was found that party politics and party discipline took over and the original concept of the Senate in that regard has gone.
May 27, 1991

We also heard the concerns of multicultural groups and women who want to see their hopes and aspirations mirrored in the Constitution. It is not going to be an easy task to resolve these interests, but we certainly must make the attempt to accommodate these various groups.
I do not believe that we should shy away from our diversity. I think that is a central facet of the Canadian character. We have searched for an identity. We are not all the same. That is what makes us different from countries such as the United States. We do not look for a melting pot. We have to celebrate our diversity and realize that it exists. Overhanging it all is the concept of Canadian citizenship. We have a great deal to be proud of in this country. We have accomplished a great deal together. We certainly are a country of geography but more and more we are country of history. We share a common history and we have to be proud of our Canadianism, recognizing the diversity which exists below it.
I think that is the way we can go to make this country a great country.
I am also confident in the idea of giving more power to backbench members of Parliament. It is something that may do a lot with regard to the regional differences in this country.
I am confident that the three main themes outlined in the Speech from the Throne are matters in which this country has to progress. The challenges have been set out well in the Speech from the Throne. It is now left to us to shoulder our responsibilities and deal with these matters in order that we may go forward as a confident, vibrant country in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to speak to the throne speech, especially since my constituency of Cariboo-Chilcotin is one of the farthest away from Ottawa. In the eyes of my constituents it is probably thousands of miles farther from Ottawa than it really is because not only in Cariboo- Chilcotin but in rural constituencies across Canada people tend to feel that the system is there for the major centres in the country and for central Canada, but it is not there when they need it for small town Canada.
When we get into a topic such as the throne speech we have people from the centre of Canada, especially from the media and the opposition, leading Canadians, talk
The Address
about its relevance, whether it is hitting the target that it was supposed to and whether it is what Canada should be dealing with over the next year or two. Many of them have been very critical. Many of them have said that it does not do the task.
It made me settle back and do a bit of thinking as to whether it did address the issues that the people in my constituency and in many other rural constituencies feel are important. I was fortunate in that over the past few weeks I had the opportunity to actually spend time with my constituents. As a western member, it takes me 24 hours to go to my riding and back on a normal trip. It is very difficult for me to get intensive time with my constituents. Over the past few weeks I had that opportunity.
I can say that the people I met with and the issues they discussed turned out to be those things that are in the throne speech. The things that were critical to the people of Cariboo-Chilcotin are in fact what is considered by this government to be critical to the people right through Canada.
I had the opportunity to deal with people in the schools, the students and the teachers. I met with business people who were concerned with the economy and employment. I met with native leaders regarding the problems that we are encountering in our area as they pertain to their aspirations and how quickly we are able to deal with them. I was able to discuss with people topics of tolerance and understanding which are not unique to that area but are qualities which are going to be required across Canada in the resolution of the major problems that we are facing today.
What are the Speech from the Throne items critical not only to us here in Ottawa but to the people in the rural ridings and in particular Cariboo-Chilcotin? I will try to go through and itemize the key themes of the speech and explain why they are critical to smaller towns and communities.
Unity: people may question whether that is the principal issue in my area because we have, technically speaking, no communities of francophones in Cariboo- Chilcotin. The people of that area are critically aware of the issues involved in this. They recognize that the resolution of this long outstanding problem is one that is going to be very important not only to Canada but to

May 27, 1991
The Address
them. We had the opportunity to address a number of groups over several days.
Something that the Speaker of this House, John Fraser, has been doing is something that I think is a real service to Canada. He has been trying, when he has time, to address groups. Some of the themes he covered in some of his addresses I would like to point out because they are the ones that some of the people in my area, especially the students and some of the business leaders, feel are critical to this debate.
The Speaker is very knowledgeable in the history of Canada and in the history of its traditions and was able to point out, like nobody else I had listened to, the bearing of history and the need for us to understand it and to know what it is telling us in trying to deal with the unity issue today. Most people, like me, when they think of Canada tend to go back to our Constitution of 1867 and deal with Canada since that time.
The Speaker in his discussion took us way back beyond that to the origins of Canada, indicating that it was the French-speaking communities with the English-speaking communities and the aboriginals who were here before us who formed the essence of what is now Canada. When the English-speaking people of Canada under the British defeated the French-speaking people of Canada on the Plains of Abraham, a remarkable thing happened. Unlike other parts of the world where vanquished and defeated people are treated like beaten people for some reason or other-I do not know the wisdom of this and some will criticize it but I will be maintaining it was a very wise move-they recognized that they did not want to treat the francophones of Canada as a beaten people.
They wanted recognition of who they were and their differences. In fact they were given four guarantees at that time: that they would be able to keep their language, religion and culture, and that they would be able to retain their legal system rather than that of the British.
Because of that decision, which many people may question, some significant things happened that in fact resulted in our ability to call ourselves Canadians today.
Shortly after that decision the American Revolution took place. At that time Canada remained strong with Britain. When I say Canada I am referring to Quebec as well.
The French speaking people of Canada honoured their alliance with the English speaking people of Canada. Because of that, history was probably changed. If the French speaking people of Quebec had sided with the American colonies, the Canada we know today would probably not have occurred.
Subsequently, in 1812 there was also the war between Canada and the United States. In fact, not too many people know that Canadians actually got as far as Washington. We were responsible for burning the White House. That is probably not something we want to brag about too much today.
In the War of 1812, because the French speaking people of Quebec had been treated with tolerance and understanding, they sided with the English speaking people of Canada. They were able to remain intact as a Canadian entity.
Since that time, we have gone through many points of history that I will not try to repeat here. The francophone communities in Quebec and in other parts of Canada, and the English speaking people in the rest of Canada, have been able to stay united and work together.
Because of the difference and the ability to work together, we have retained Canada as it is today, the Canada that we know. Because our ancestors were able to do that, that is the reason why we, not only in the House of Commons but right across the country, must and will ensure that Canada remains intact during our tenure here. That will probably be decided over the next few years.
The unity issue goes beyond just the Quebec fact. I think everybody has realized that. Whereas the Meech Lake discussion did deal and was trying to address the problem with the Quebec issue, we have gone way beyond that now.
In dealing with the fact of unity this year and next year, we must be concerned with dealing fairly and properly with the province of Quebec. It also entails being fair and equitable, and dealing with honour with all the other regions of Canada.
May 27, 1991

Today, nobody thinks we are going to be able to resolve the issue of Canada and its unity by dealing strictly with the issues in Quebec. In many people's minds, the issues pushing up in other parts of Canada, such as British Columbia and the western regions, are just as, if not more, critical. If we do not find solutions to these problems, the reasons for the feeling of alienation by the people in the west and other parts of Canada, we do not have a chance of finding unity for the rest of the country.
It is not just Quebec now. We are able to deal with the regions. Anybody in today's forum realizes that if we do not deal fairly and equitably with the natives, our aboriginal peoples, we will not be able to reach a consensus.
I will deal with the issue of government reform briefly. It is of interest to the people of small communities such as those in Cariboo-Chilcotin. To a great extent, their inability to relate to us here in Ottawa on how we operate is causing many of the problems throughout the country. They are sick and tired of the partisanship, not just from the opposition parties, but from all parties of this House. They want to know that the members who are sitting in this House are representing them in an honest, proper and respectful manner. Any of the steps that we take, as members of Parliament, to achieve greater respect for the people in this House by our constituents is very critical.
One of the members opposite is saying: "Talk to your side of the House". Yes, we will talk to our side of the House and I hope that he will talk to the people on his side of the House. It is all of us together that will be needed to make these changes, but it is the people of Canada that will be the great beneficiaries because they deserve a better system than they have now.
When it comes to the economic competitiveness that was highlighted in the Speech from the Throne, the people in my area of Cariboo-Chilcotin could write the book on this. They cannot survive unless they are economically competitive. In fact, the principal industry in Cariboo-Chilcotin is the principal industry of Canada. It is the forest industry.
The Address
In fact, we produce in Cariboo-Chilcotin 7 or 8 per cent of all of the softwood lumber that is produced in Canada. We cannot think of the economic situation without thinking about world markets, the Pacific Rim, the U.S. and the European markets. We cannot think about those unless we as a nation, and we as a people in our area are truly competitive. It has been in a world market situation for years and years. It is because of that that the industry in our area has responded.
I can remember during the 1981-82 recession the changes the forest industry in British Columbia went through. The changes that they had to make in the subsequent six and seven years to remain competitive on a world basis were substantial. They have totally transformed how they operate. In fact, they are a world class producer. They can compete with anyone on the world in their products. That of course is the ability that we require right across this great land of ours. All of our industries that can be competitive must be. That of course is the issue being addressed in the throne speech.
I could go on, but I would like to start to wrap up now with what I consider to be the most important message that we could bring to Canada during this throne speech; that is, how are we going to be able to achieve the resolution of the major problems that we are facing. I maintain that we have to find a way to change the national self-image.
I am a parent, I was an educator at one time. I think anyone who has been in either of those positions realizes that we cannot create strong children or strong students unless they have a positive self-image. They have to start believing in themselves and in their abilities.
As a nation we seem to have taken a totally opposite tack. Every time I look around I see people telling us why we as Canadians are failures, why we as Canadians cannot succeed. We are told through the media and by so many of our leaders that environmentally we are backward, environmentally we are offenders in the world environment. That is absolutely untrue. We are one of the most significant nations in the world in addressing the problems of the environment and succeeding in it. We have thousands of examples of where we are doing things that no other nation has been able to achieve. We very seldom talk about them.

May 27, 1991
The Address
When it comes to our attitude as a nation regarding our competitiveness, we are continually being told that we cannot compete, that we need to put up barriers to try to protect our industries and our people. That is implying that we do not have the ability to compete with nations around the world. That is absolutely not the case.
To return to my riding, I would like to close with two points. I travelled through my riding from the north end to the south. There are many communities but farther south they tend to have more and more extreme economic problems. I went to Litton, which is at the veiy southern end of the riding in the middle of the Fraser Canyon. It is a very small community. It has basically two industries: ginseng, which employs very few people, and a sawmill.
Just one week prior to my visit one of our national banks found it necessary to remove the sawmill's line of credit. Of course it had to shut down. It did not have the cash flow to continue. This mill employs in the neighbourhood of 100 people directly and half of those people are native Indians who are totally dependent on the income they receive from it.
When I arrived in that town I expected the attitude to be one of gloom and doom. I expected to be hit with all of the problems the town was facing and demands for me to come up with solutions that I would not be able to provide. It was exactly the opposite. I went to that town and met with the native leaders, the leaders of the town, and the people from the mill. I did hear briefly about some of their problems.
However, the people spent more time talking about some of the solutions to those problems. They spoke of how the community like it never had before, natives and non-natives alike, was pulling together to try to resolve the economic and social problems it faced. That is an example of one small town in Cariboo-Chilcotin that is a model for all of us in Canada to follow.
My last point is to indicate again how small town Canada can help to show us the way. We have heard much said about the intolerance of Canada, especially as it pertains to the new situation concerning the RCMP officer who recently graduated. That graduate is going to be serving his first duty in a town in my riding. It was with great pride that I read several articles in the paper, one
editorial in particular, which indicated that in this small town of the Cariboo we were going to be able to show the public of Canada what real tolerance, tolerance at the street to street, block to block, neighbour to neighbour level really means. It is going to be happening in Quesnel, British Columbia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for speaking up for rural Canada in this House and letting us know a little bit about the views and ideas of his constituents.
I have a similar rural riding to his. I too have been through my riding asking my people their views on Canada, the future of Canada, and where we are going as nation. Some of the issues they talk to me about, I am sure he also runs into in his riding.
I am wondering if we could exchange notes. Possibly we could share and talk about some of the solutions put forward by his constituents.
One of the important matters concerning rural Canadians in my riding is the economic situation of rural Canada and the effect that the high Canadian dollar and high interest rates have had on rural Canada, especially the agricultural industries. I also have some ginseng growers in my riding, as does the hon. member. My riding is mostly tobacco, ginseng, cash crops and supply managed crops. My agricultural constituents are really concerned about the effects the high dollar and interest rates are having on all their products and the uncertainty in the international community regarding the GATT negotiations.
Another of the areas that many of my entrepreneurs and small businesses talked about were the effects of the GST on them doing business. Even talking to students going through the schools, the first thing they brought up was the effect the GST was having on them buying certain materials they need not only for their schooling, but in their day-to-day lives.
The other thing that was talked about a lot in my riding was the closing of rural post offices, rural post offices being the significant spot in many of our rural communities where the federal government is represented. What rural Canadians were saying on the post office issue was that they wanted fair treatment with urban Canadians in terms of having a postal service in their communities.
May 27, 1991

These are some of the issues being brought up in my community, and I am sure the hon. member heard these same concerns in his riding.
In terms of native issues, I have a large native constituency in my riding: the Six Nations, the Mississau-gas and the New Credit. They were really concerned that no action had been taken in some time regarding the issue of land claims and Indian self-government.
I want to have the member's comments on these areas. Maybe he could tell us some of the solutions he has come up with.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for the positive way in which he has actually brought his questions out.
It is interesting that we both represent rural communities but, in many ways, there are differences from one rural community to another. I will try to highlight some of them.
The impact of the U.S. dollar, the high value of the Canadian dollar versus the U.S. dollar, is of critical importance to the people of Cariboo-Chilcotin. Obviously most of our economy is based on the exporting of softwood lumber and it is based in U.S. dollars no matter where we sell it in the world. It has been a problem for some time. Of course the critical problem with the lumber industry is world trade and the world markets. They realize that. The demand has to be there. When you get into times like we are in now, that does have a critical impact.
I have explored for many years any ways in which we could, as a country, try to influence the dollar. I had an economist address it for me recently. I asked him specifically if there were more things we could do to reduce the dollar. The answer I got was: "You could do minor things, but basically the reason why we have a high dollar is because the people in this world have confidence in the Canadian dollar as an investment." It is foreigners investing in the Canadian dollar that is driving it up. I do not think that is something that you and I would really want to change overnight, even though the high dollar is critical to us.
I agree with your point on the high interest rate. The high interest rates there have been over the past year has affected the people in my area, not nearly as much as it
The Address
did a few years ago when the interest rates went out of control, but they definitely have affected them. However, I really believe that we should not be talking about high interest rates right now. Our interest rates now are very reasonable. We have the lowest interest rates now that we have had for years and years. There is not an industry in the country that would say we cannot exist or compete with the interest rates we have now.
Our job in this House and as a government is try to ensure that we retain those low interest rates. To do that, we have to follow with the restraint program that we are following and, of course, take all of the steps that are possible and necessary to keep the inflationary heat out of our economy.
Another issue you hit on was the GST. It was brought up in my visits to my constituency. In the opinions I received, it was not critical to any of the industries in a negative sense. It was a frustration adapting to.
There are still many things that we have to do to make it work better.
Most of them, especially in the business communities, recognize the reasons for it. We are a province that has to export, and exporters realize that the manufacturers' sales tax did hurt us and that the goods and service tax, no matter how annoying it is, is there to make us more competitive, to help us in our world trading.
I have 60,000 square miles of rural Canada in my riding. Obviously, I have many, many post offices, some the normal variety of post offices run by Canada Post, but many have been modernized and turned over to free enterprise. In a few communities some people are terribly upset with the situation. Most have accepted it, and feel in many cases they are doing a better job.
Some communities resent terribly not so much what has happened but the way it has happened. They have not had a chance to have the input that they would like. But in most cases the post office, which is a critical element of every one of these small communities, is functioning well in my area. We had problems a year or so ago, but basically they seem to be not only happy with it but in many cases are indicating that some of the changes that have taken place have, in fact, made the service better, better in a way they had not realized before.

May 27, 1991
The Address
You closed on the issue as it pertains to the native Indians in your riding and in mine. Of course in British Columbia we have never had, except for a few isolated examples, any treaties. So within British Columbia the issue of Indian land claims, Indian title, Indian rights, is a critical issue today. I spent many hours last summer at blockades in various parts of my riding. They were not as large as the ones you encountered in Quebec and central Canada, but no less critical to us out there. The issue is one about which the native leaders that I met with are cautiously optimistic with respect to the role the federal government is playing now. They see the negotiation process taking place in British Columbia and they see that they have their involvement in it.
I would say that scepticism is still there, but they are cautiously optimistic that we are dealing with their issues in a proper manner now.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the final day of the special debate on the throne speech which was presented on May 13, 1991. We have had six days of debate on the speech, but there has been nothing said so far by the Prime Minister or any of his ministers to try to explain or justify its contents that changes the essential reality. The Speech from the Throne is an admission by the government of just how precarious a situation we have in this country, a situation that has been created in large measure by this government.
The Prime Minister says the problem is that Canadians are lacking in patriotism and they should be more enthusiastic about their country. Well I say that Canadians are not lacking in patriotism or in enthusiasm for their country, they are lacking enthusiasm for this government and its policies, which are undoing the very fabric of our nation.
It is difficult for a lot of Canadians to have faith in the future of their country when they are uncertain about their own economic future.
In this throne speech, the government appears to have finally realized that there is an important link between the economy and national unity.

My party and myself have been saying for a long time that a strong economy gives a boost to national unity and that Canada can only achieve its maximum potential in an increasingly competitive global economy as a strong and unified nation.
Unfortunately, the government has not provided a clear and meaningful economic agenda in this throne speech. Three months ago, Canadians hoped this government would provide a new plan for economic recovery in its February 1991 budget. In fact, Liberals called for such a plan. It was nowhere to be found then and it is nowhere to be found now.
At the time of the February 1991 budget, just three months ago, the government said that inflation is economic enemy number one and must be kept in check with high interest rates. However, in the throne speech on May 13 we were told, and I quote: "economic recovery depends on reducing interest rates".
This latter day conversion may signal that the government is finally willing to recognize that economic damage is caused by fighting inflation solely with high interest rates and by making the fight against inflation a higher priority than job creation and economic growth. It may signal that the government is ready to consider other ways of dealing with inflation, ways that will not have the disastrous side effects of massive job losses and a shrinking economy produced by this government's present policies.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is not the only country to want a low and stable inflation rate but it is certainly the only one prepared to achieve this goal at any cost!
The Economic Council of Canada has been keeping a close eye on the experience of countries such as Austria, Norway, Sweden, West Germany and Japan which have managed to control inflationary pressures somewhat without a drastic increase in their level of unemployment.

The Economic Council of Canada, the government's own advisory body, identified in the other countries I have listed what it called a "social partnership" among business, labour and government. This social partnership, the council said: "seems to offer the key to controlling inflation without creating an unacceptable level of unemployment".

The partnership is based on compromise among the three players on a wide range of economic policy issues and, the council adds, it must begin with a political commitment on the part of the government to full employment. There has been no such commitment from this government, not in the budget and certainly not in this throne speech.
Without consultations on economic goals with all of Canada's economic stakeholders, we must fear that the Bank of Canada, with the support of the government, will continue to fight inflation principally with the blunt instrument of high interest rates and ignore the economic and human costs of lost jobs and lost business activity.
This means that the government would be relying on the very policies that got us into the recession to now get us out of it. That simply does not make much sense.
In the throne speech the government says it wants to create 2.5 million jobs by the year 2000, nine years from now. At first glance, that looks pretty good on paper. However, on closer examination it is clear that the government has set its sights extremely low. Even the finance minister's own department confirms that between 1970 and 1979, more than 10 years ago, the same number of jobs, 2.5 million, were created in a much smaller economy. In that nine year period, from 1970 to 1979, economic growth averaged 4.7 per cent, significantly more than the 4.0 per cent growth rate for the period up to 1995, as predicted in the budget of last February.

This government also failed, Mr. Speaker, to mention in the Speech from the Throne the other economic factors to be considered to get to this 2.5 million jobs figure. Without any indication of the projected population growth or labour force involvement, for instance, the job creation forecast by this govemement in the Speech from the Throne is not of much value.

For example, Canada could create 2.5 million jobs by the year 2000, but still have double digit unemployment of more than 10 per cent. Would this percentage level be acceptable? The government's answer cannot be found clearly stated in the throne speech. However, by setting
The Address
out these targets, it looks like a 10 per cent unemployment level would be acceptable to this government.
I am sure the answer of Canadians is that this level is simply not acceptable. They would not want this to be the target of the government. They would not want this goal to be in effect 10 or 20 years from now. The government should realize that simply setting as a goal something that could happen anyway is just not good enough. Canadians deserve better.
What about the nearly 1.5 million people who are looking for work and need a job right now? What about those people who have lost their jobs permanently through plant closings? What about the job requirements of a growing population? If the government had wanted to back up its words on job creation, we would have seen a commitment to full employment in the throne speech. The 1.5 million Canadians now looking for work deserve such a commitment. This government has an obligation to provide this commitment and to work at starting to carry it out right now.

Mr. Speaker, government policies must ensure coordination among the various factors which will put us in a competitive position-interest rates, tax system and other policies-if we want to achieve sustained economic growth.

The throne speech identifies the importance to Canadians of being able to compete effectively in international markets. Speaking of guaranteeing our economic future, the government says we should begin by "equipping ourselves to compete with the best."
These are beautiful words, but they ring hollow when they come from a government that has decreased its own spending on research and development as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product-the over-all size of the economy-every year since 1986, especially after the Prime Minister had promised to double the level of spending on research and development in this country.
The former Minister of Finance, now the Minister for International Trade, has admitted that: "Canada's investment in research and development has been low by the standards of the main industrialized countries". It was his own budgets that in effect cut spending on

The Address
research and development and science and technology programs.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association says that Canada's ability to compete with its major trading partners is only 85 per cent of what it was in 1980, with most of the reduction occurring in the last half of that decade since this Conservative government came to power. Canada, which relies on exports for almost 30 per cent of its prosperity, has lost 20 per cent of its share of world markets in the last five years and its share of world export trade fell from 5 per cent to 4 per cent.
Fundamental to any country's ability to compete are its exchange rates and its interest rates. Business leaders in our export sector, one of the cornerstones of our economy, continue to identify the high Canadian dollar and high interest rates as key contributors to Canada's declining competitiveness. In addition to helping bring down the value of the Canadian dollar, lower interest rates would also make it easier for companies to make the capital investments necessary to bring about higher productivity and to become more competitive.
Other factors in becoming more competitive include a country's tax system and the quality of its human capital-its people. Government policy must ensure that the ingredients for becoming more competitive are co-ordinated with business and labour to help achieve long-run productivity growth.
The throne speech waxes eloquent about the need for Canada to invest in its people-its human capital. The government already had an opportunity to do something about it three months earlier in its February budget. What did we see? Not only no new programs to help Canadian workers gain the skills they would need to compete with skilled workers from other countries, but we saw that the government actually cut $100 million from its Canada Jobs Strategy. The throne speech did nothing at all to make up for that omission.

Of course, Mr. Speaker, even before we can become internationally competitive, we should take a close look at our national stakes. In the Speech from the Throne, the government was forced in fact to admit that "regulations [-Jmake it simpler for producers to ship their
products abroad than to sell them in neighbouring provinces."

The throne speech calls for an end to interprovincial trade barriers by 1995. This is a worth-while objective but the government set out no clear plan of action on how to reach it.
In 1987, before the government concluded its free trade negotiations with the Americans, Liberals called for a reduction in interprovincial trade barriers within Canada. We believed then as we believe now that our first priority should be free trade here at home-right here in Canada. Why should we embark on discussions for a trade deal with Mexico before we have created conditions for free trade here in Canada?
The same high interest rate policy of this government which has helped undermine our ability to compete has also helped drive up the Canadian dollar to its highest level in years. This, in combination with the GST and other tax policies of the federal government-not to mention the higher gasoline and other taxes imposed by the new NDP government in Ontario-is helping to create an unprecedented exodus of Canadian shoppers to the United States.
It is estimated that in Ontario alone cross-border shopping will result in about $1 billion in lost retail sales this year, representing up to $80 million in lost provincial tax revenues and corresponding, or perhaps larger amounts in federal tax revenues.
I am told that in Kingston, Ontario, a community of about 100,000 people, a report for its Chamber of Commerce by the accounting firm, Ernst and Young, says that cross-border shopping will cost the area 500 jobs and cost local merchants $78 million in lost sales. Kingston is about one hour away from the nearest major American city.
Let us take a look at Windsor, Ontario, 10 minutes away from a major American city. A recent study by the University of Windsor suggests that Windsor and the surrounding Essex County could lose as many as 4,600 jobs and $281 million from their local economy this year alone, all due to the direct and indirect effects of cross-border shopping.
The number of Canadians making day trips to the United States increased 30 per cent in 1990 and is expected to increase even more this year.
May 27, 1991

In Windsor, this past March, more than 25,000 people paid duty at the bridge and at the tunnel. That is an increase of more than 500 per cent from April 1988 when just over 4,000 paid duty. In spite of this increase, the president of the Customs and Excise union local in Windsor says that at times the customs officers are so swamped that they just wave through passengers in cars who would otherwise have to stop and pay duty on their United States purchases. Sometimes as many as six in ten cars are waved through.
This government has not only created the cross-border shopping problem with its policies. It willingly allows thousands of dollars in duties and taxes to go uncollected every day. Canada Customs must be given the resources to properly staff border crossing points. The idea here is not to have some kind of border police force, but rather to make it smooth and efficient for those Canadians who shop in the United States to pay the duties and taxes they owe. It is only fair because these duties and taxes are in effect collected on the same kind of goods when they are sold right here in Canada.
The fact that the provincial sales tax is not collected upon entry into Canada also adds to the uneven playing field that presently exists.
The Minister of National Revenue tries to say that this cannot be done, that collecting two kinds of retail sales taxes on two different sets of items is too complex. He says he will collect the Ontario tax only if it is changed and harmonized with the federal GST, that is, if it is imposed on all the same items in the same way. This is nonsense.
All the minister has to do is go to any store in Ontario and he will find clerks with relatively little training and experience who are dealing with these same two taxes in their current form day in and day out, calculating them and applying them to the right products in the right way. If these retail clerks can do it so can our more highly trained Customs officers if our Minister of National Revenue will tell them to do it.
After all, our Customs officers are already collecting provincial taxes for the Ontario government on liquor brought in by individuals without any problem and
The Address
without these taxes being first harmonized with federal taxes on liquor.
Why is the Minister of National Revenue hesitating? I think it is because he wants to use the issue of the provincial sales tax at the border as a form of political blackmail designed to get the Ontario government to bring in its own form of GST. That is wrong. The federal GST is already enough of a burden without the minister and this Conservative government trying to create more GST at the provincial level.
Furthermore, the federal government and the Government of Ontario should not be so quick to dismiss the idea put forward by border community mayors of differential gasoline taxes in areas close to the American border. After all, a system like that has been operating with provincial gasoline taxes in Quebec for many years. This would certainly go a long way toward making the playing field level for Canadians.

speechtext: Agreed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude by saying that with respect to the current concern about negotiations with the United States on the matter of trade with the United States and with Mexico, we know that in order to get approval from the Congress for fast-track negotiations President Bush promised that before any deal with Mexico would be signed there would be adjustment programs for workers who would lose their jobs because of a new trilateral free trade deal involving Mexico. He promised that companies would not be able to use any trade deal with Mexico to get around tougher environmental and labour laws in the United States.
There have been no such commitments from our government and there should be. Adjustment programs were promised by the Prime Minister during the debate over the last trade deal, the one with the United States. After the deal was signed he backed down on that promise. We now see the resulting economic damage in terms of lost jobs and closed plants day after day.

The Address
No wonder we in the Official Opposition question why Canada should be at the table with Mexico and the United States at all unless and until these questions and uncertainties are clearly and positively dealt with.
I say by way of conclusion that it is not good enough for the government to talk in its throne speech about how great the economy will be eventually. This talk has to be backed up by policies that reinforce our national institutions and by policies that help create strong and swift economic growth.
In order for Canada to remain united it is important that Canadians have confidence in the economic future of their country. That is why we Liberals have been calling for policies that will help us restructure and modernize our firms and retrain our work force.
These steps are truly needed to increase our competitiveness so that we can have strong companies and strong growth in both jobs and output all on a long-term continuing basis.
There are some Canadians who say that at present we should focus only, or at least mainly, on the economy and on developing and implementing those government policies that would help get it moving again. However, Canadians cannot expect to get help from their national government unless we continue to have a country, one united country, from coast to coast to coast.
Therefore, along with giving priority to our economic problems, we must at the same time pay attention to concerns about national unity. Let us also recognize that we cannot have an effective united country without an effective national government.
By strengthening our economic base and our unity as a country, we will be making the best possible preparation for the challenges of the future.
This throne speech does not help us to make such preparations and, therefore, deserves to be rejected by this House and by the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most pleased to listen to my colleague from Windsor West stating the case for Windsor with respect to the question of cross-border shopping with emphasis on the number of Canadians who are shopping in Detroit which, if you time your entry into Detroit correctly, you can get there in five minutes rather than ten.
I wonder if my colleague would elaborate a bit not just on the issue of Canadians going into Detroit but on the effect of government policies on the movement of Americans into Windsor and the impact there is on the retail trade and recreational establishments in Windsor which a few years ago were doing quite well with tourism.
To pursue a quite separate and distinct issue with respect to the throne speech, I would be interested in hearing my colleague comment on an omission from the throne speech.
In spite of the suggestion of targets for education and training there was no mention whatever of research and development targets, in spite of the promise of the Prime Minister in 1983 that the percentage of the Gross Domestic Product expended in Canada on R and D must be doubled.
There is also the fact that in other contexts it is widely reported that the government has abandoned all targets whatever for R and D, so I would like to hear his comments on the impact of that significant policy omission and policy change with respect to economic development.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague has raised an important point.
There is a very substantial hospitality industry in the Windsor and Essex County area catering to Americans who come over to shop, to dine in our restaurants and to spend a day touring our various places of interest. This industry has been severely damaged by the GST and earlier by the high dollar.
These additional costs have been discouraging Americans from coming over as they have been for years to dine in our restaurants, to shop in our stores, and to visit our tourist attractions. These are mainly day trips.
They are further discouraged by the high volume of traffic at the bridge and the tunnel which causes them to have to wait in line for several hours, sometimes, before they can get across.
This is another reason why we need more staff at these major border crossing points and why there have to be provisions, as we find in a number of international airports outside Canada, where people, like Americans coming to Windsor to shop or to dine who have nothing to declare should be dealt with separately and differently
May 27, 1991

from people who are returning and have to be examined for purchases they made and for duties they owe.
This is an important aspect of the whole problem of cross-border shopping. The government needs to take action on this problem before more permanent damage is done to the economy, not just that of Windsor and Essex County but of all Canada. Most of our population lives within a short drive to the American border. The whole economy is affected by this problem being allowed to drag on without more effective action being taken.
Furthermore, if this government is interested in making Canada more competitive, then the throne speech should have set out some clear targets and objectives for improving the performance of the economy when it comes to research and development and science and technology. All we have so far are the cutbacks in recent budgets by this government of support for private sector and university initiatives in research and development and science and technology. This is not the way to make this country more competitive.
I regret that the throne speech has not corrected the errors of past budgets in this regard. I hope there will be action taken before long, because our country needs to work together, with business and labour supported by government, to improve the level of its competitiveness. That means new and improved government policies when it comes to research and development and science and technology.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour and a great privilege to rise today as a participant in this historic throne speech debate.
This debate is about the future of a great nation. This debate is about a vision of a stronger Canada for our children. This debate is about building a better Canada for all Canadians from sea to sea to shining sea.
The Speech from the Throne serves as a foundation and is a critical element in the success of our nation. It demonstrates the commitment of our government to Canadian unity, prosperity and responsiveness.
The issue of Canadian unity is an important one. Canadians are now at a turning point in their history. This country is a great nation. We have constructed a country with generations of men and women determined to make a home for themselves and a future for their
The Address
children. Tolerance and fairness, courage and compassion, individual enterprise and neighbourly co-operation have always succeeded in overcoming obstacles and erasing doubt.
Now is the time for us to use these skills to strengthen Canada so that it can meet the challenges of the 21st century.
While we know that a country is more than just a constitution, we also know that a constitution should unite a nation. Canadians across this country should see themselves and their hopes and aspirations mirrored in their constitution. That is not the case today. Therefore, no other task is more crucial than making the constitution more relevant to the citizens, the peoples of the various regions of this country.
Many agree that the final constitutional product is vital for Canada's success. However, it is becoming increasingly more clear that what is also important is the constitutional process. All Canadians must have the opportunity to participate in this process. All Canadians need to get involved so that our way of life can be preserved and enhanced for future generations.
Federal, provincial and territorial governments are now engaged in consulting Canadians on different aspects of making changes to the Constitution. At the federal level, the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future was created to bring Canadians together to talk about the fundamental values and characteristics of Canada.
Parliamentary committees will continue to consult Canadians to find better ways of making constitutional changes. Through these mechanisms and processes Canadians are now developing a consensus about the basic values and aspirations that should underlie constitutional reform.
All of this contributes to an increased understanding among Canadians of how much we have in common as well as an awareness of what we stand to lose. Once we have heard an as broad as possible range of views, and only after receiving and considering the summations and reports of the public commissions and parliamentary committees, the government will propose a plan for a renewed Canada to the people of Canada.

May 27, 1991
The Address
Our government is committed to Canadian unity, but the job of attaining that worth-while goal is not a task for government alone. Canadian unity will be achieved only through a combined effort of all Canadians working together for a better future. Canadian unity will be realized when Canadians recognize and accommodate each other's differences while at the same time focusing and building on our similarities. Together we will build a better Canada.
Our government, in addition to being committed to Canadian unity, is also committed to securing Canada's prosperity.
Canada has one of the highest standards of living in the world and a quality of life second to none. There is no guarantee that such progress will continue. Simply relying on the things that have helped us succeed in the past will not be enough to improve further our material welfare and quality of life.
Restoring economic growth is essential. We must go beyond this to attain economic prosperity. Canadians must work more effectively together in a partnership for prosperity to meet Canada's competitive challenge. As the world economy becomes increasingly more competitive, Canada has been falling behind its trading partners in its ability to compete in the global marketplace.
The most telling indicator of Canada's future economic challenges is its productivity performance. Unfortunately, our productivity performance-how efficiently we produce goods and services-has been deteriorating.
The 1984 agenda for economic renewal outlined the competitive challenge facing Canada and subsequent actions helped to provide a better framework for restoring productivity growth. Today Canadians are increasingly concerned about their ability to compete. These concerns range from broad economic issues such as inflation, interest rates and the exchange rate, to problems with our productivity performance like the effectiveness of investments, the burden of government and the business climate.
Governments have a responsibility to create an environment that encourages the growth of competitive and successful enterprise. The 1991 budget announced actions to restore fiscal balance and move toward price stability. This will lead to a stable broad economic environment, increased confidence in the Canadian
economy and will strengthen Canada's ability to compete in a touch economic world.
Boosting productivity growth and prosperity is far more than a job just for government. The private sector must take full advantage of the opportunities created by the actions of governments. In order to maximize productivity growth, the quality of investments in infrastructure, machinery, equipment, training, education and research and technology must be scrutinized. As well, consideration must be given to private sector spending in the areas of training and research, and to other areas such as education where, by international standards, Canada's level of spending compares well but its performance does not.
Prosperity and competitiveness are not only issues for business, labour and government. All Canadians can help to strengthen Canada's competitive ability by identifying and developing an awareness of the problems. Only then can they be a part of developing solutions.
I would like to conclude by discussing another very important issue to Canadians, and that is Canadians and their environment. Canadians do care about their environment and are concerned that it is preserved and protected. We are all taking action to protect it and are personally involved in finding solutions.
Canada's green plan is a comprehensive $3 billion action plan which expresses this government's commitment to work with Canadians to manage our resources prudently and to encourage sensitive environmental decision-making. The green plan is proof that the government is listening and responding to the environmental concerns of Canadians. It was developed as a result of extensive consultation with Canadians from all walks of life. It is timely, responsive and sensitive to the needs of Canadians. The government has forged a series of environmental partnerships beginning with individuals and ranging through special interest groups and the private sector as well as municipal and provincial governments. Environmental partnerships extend to the international level as well.
Canada's green plan provides Canadians with information to help them make informed decisions about the state of the environment and to help them understand what we as individuals and as a nation can do in addressing the problems. We realize that unilateral action in itself will not solve all environmental problems. Solutions require everyone's involvement and everyone
May 27, 1991

has a part to play so that we may live in a clean and healthy environment now and in the future.
In conclusion, the Government of Canada in its Speech from the Throne has demonstrated and reaffirmed its commitment to national unity, to economic prosperity and to responsiveness to Canadians. The challenges that the country and the government face are serious challenges and they are challenges that are not unknown in other counties around the world. When we look around the globe, we see other challenges in countries like South America and the Soviet Union, countries having difficulties with violence. When we view all of that and we consider the situation in Canada, we recognize that we do live in a great nation but that we have a lot of room to grow and the challenges are great. These challenges will not be met with an ununified effort.
