speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to start by congratulating the hon. member on a well done presentation.
In his speech he spoke a little bit about the comparative position of Canada internationally and he stressed the importance of education and research and development as a means of improving competitiveness. These are very good comments, they are excellent comments.
I would like to add one dimension to this whole debate and that is the productivity question, which has been coming up on a regular basis in discussions. I might suggest that you can put all of the money you want into education and research and development but productivity by itself is not going to improve. Productivity will only improve in Canada if we are able to remove all of the barriers between the provinces and if we are able to ensure and secure a market for corporations and companies which produce goods.
The reason I say this is because one of the reasons Canadian goods are more expensive than American or other goods is because many of the companies that produce those goods have short runs on those goods. For
The Address
example, a company that manufactures chairs, plates pens or pencils will produce for a local market. If the market can bear 100,000 pens or 100,000 plates, the company would produce that quantity, while other corporations might enjoy bigger markets and perhaps produce 500,000 or 1,000,000.
As a result of that, the unit price will be reduced and the consumer will get the benefit of that reduction.
I want to hear the comments of my colleagues on the question of removing the barriers between the provinces and the target of 1995, which is very far off and should be moved up.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. colleague from Ottawa for posing such a thoughtful question. Indeed, the trade barriers between provinces are certainly an obstacle to increasing our economic growth. There are a number of things that can be done to address that concern.
We could eliminate a number of things. We could eliminate the policies that favour one province's suppliers over lower cost producers from other provinces. We need to eliminate regulations that often make it simpler for producers to ship their products abroad than to sell them in neighbouring provinces. We need to eliminate hiring policies that give preference to provincial residents over those from other provinces. We also need to eliminate occupational standards that restrict work opportunities for residents of other provinces.
One recent estimate put the number of barriers to interprovincial trade in Canada at approximately 500. The government's goal is to see barriers to interprovincial trade, services and investment come down by 1995 to allow Canada to become a single integrated market.
The savings to taxpayers and consumers of creating such a market could be as high as $6 billion, about $1,000 a year for a household of four. Further, today investment and technology flow with ease across international boundaries, markets for goods and services are specialized, and decisions on production are made on a worldwide basis.

May 27, 1991
The Address
I agree with the hon. member that one of the major issues that the Canadian government should address is interprovincial trade barriers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to rise and say a few words on the throne speech. The throne speech is an occasion for members to give some of their personal views and their advice to the Prime Minister and the cabinet.
I, first of all, would like to commend the Prime Minister and his cabinet, as well as the government caucus, for taking some very tough decisions over the last six years and sticking with them. The government needs to be commended for its goals in this throne speech: to emphasize national unity-on which I will say a few words-and to talk about maintaining our high Canadian standard of living, and indeed increasing it.
The fact of the matter is that, even with all of the problems that we have, when we look at Canada vis-avis all the other countries of the world, we come off very well. There are two external measures which we should never forget about. The first measure is the tens of millions of people trying to get into this wonderful country as refugees, often at great personal risk to themselves. There are many thousands each year who are drowned in boats and killed trying to get to safe haven countries like Canada. As well, there are the tens of millions who are trying to come as immigrants. That is an external measure of how well we have done in this country.
I often think that it is the result of the media which constantly are stressing the negative, constantly stressing the very legitimate points of conflict between our ethnic communities in Canada, between our federal government and our provincial governments, and between our regions. That is constantly emphasized by the national media and, indeed, is constantly emphasized here. The problem is that once we permitted television in the House, these conflicts were aggravated because we all play to the television, rather than address the problem. As a result, people tend to forget that Canada is really doing a lot better than we realize, and the immigrants are proof.
The second external measure is the recent study by the United Nations. Nobody can claim that the United Nations is trying to help Prime Minister Mulroney and his cabinet, but the fact of the matter is that when it
measured the human development index for 160 countries of the world-which measures such things as literacy, life expectancy and personal basic disposable income-Canada finished second out of all the countries in the world. That is an external measurement which tells me that as a nation we are doing far better than we are prepared to even give ourselves credit for.
My comments concern that. Frankly, I think Canada has proven itself. I cannot imagine why we, as a people, would permit any group of extremists, whether they are in Quebec or in western Canada, to break this wonderful country up. The one thing that is crystal clear is that if we break this country up we will all be substantially poorer and, for many years, will have an enormous problem trying to redefine ourselves. If Quebec separates then the natives might separate from Quebec and the Out-aouais might separate from Quebec.
In the west, southeastern B.C. has often wanted to be part of Alberta and in the Peace River country there are similar pressures on the opposite side.
When my eastern European constituents come up to me, they say: "Mr. Thacker, don't mess around with your borders because once you start doing that it is a never-ending process." We could break right down into individual cities wanting to be separated. We cannot have that. This is a wonderful country and we have to work together to keep it together.
The Prime Minister deserves more credit than he gets for the leadership he has provided to this country. The courage he has shown and maintained is really quite extraordinary. He deserves credit because he has his cabinet and his caucus behind him. The government caucus deserves credit if we look at reality.
In 1984 we came to power with a certain set of policies. People, whether from the C.D. Howe Institute, the Economic Council or the Department of Finance, have done extrapolations. If we had carried on with those policies from 1984 to today, the deficit would be over $70 billion and the national debt would be well over $500 billion. Obviously there had to be changes.
The opposition has opposed every tax increase, every cut in spending and, yet, had it been in power it would have had to make similar types of choices. The opposition might have acted slightly different, but we could not have permitted the policies of 1984 to continue because we would have a 50 cent dollar. Anybody who thinks their nation is richer when its dollar drops in value just
May 27, 1991

does not understand the reality of economics and does not know the examples of many other countries which have tried to lower their dollar. It might help for a month or two, but beyond that it is a disaster. Countries have to face up to their basic underlying, structural problems, they have to meet the world economy as it is rather than as they think it ought to be. That is the real problem for so many countries, they have not faced the world as it is.
I believe the Prime Minister deserves a lot more credit for the free trade agreement, the GST and, in this throne speech, the comments concerning education.
We know that education is entirely a provincial jurisdiction, but it is also clear that if the Fathers of Confederation were putting the country together today, they would have given power to the federal government over post-secondary education because that is an area where we are not getting enough specialization and graduates to cope with the world. The reason is quite simple, we have 10 countries with regard to post-secondary education and there is enormous overlap and duplication. We need to have a much stronger Canadian hat vis-a-vis education. Unfortunately, the Constitution does not call for that, but we as a national Parliament have to provide leadership. That is what this throne speech does.
Also, for the first time, the national Parliament is starting to say: "Look, provinces, you have turned this country into 10 separate nations vis-a-vis provincial economic development and provincial rules on regulation of industry." We have more barriers to the free transfer of goods and people and commodities in this country than they do in Europe where they are separate nations. Imagine Europe, where they were killing millions 50 years ago, now have fewer barriers to the transfer of money, capital, labour and educated people than we do in this country, which is supposed to be a common market.
I blame this Parliament and I blame past governments, most of whom were Liberal, because the national government should have been stopping these provincial rules that have blocked this nation from being a common market.
The Address
Section 121 of our Constitution clearly sets out that Canada is a common market. This Parliament should have been blocking these rules by using the power of disallowance, for one thing, to keep goods and capital flowing freely across this country. We must start to address that problem and it will take a few years to work it out.
My last point is vis-a-vis the Constitution. Mr. Speaker, why are we in this position? It is because in 1931, Canada became a sovereign nation in every respect except one, the amending of our Constitution. Our previous leaders in this country could not agree on an amending formula. Every Prime Minister since then has tried to patriate the Constitution and come up with an amending formula; whether it was Mackenzie King, St. Laurent, Diefenbaker, Pearson, or Trudeau in the 1970s. When they could not get unanimity, they all properly backed off because the country was being built, it was growing and we still had the second highest standard of living in the world.
Mr. Trudeau decided in 1980, when he got his last majority, to change that. He virtually forced through a patriation of the Constitution as well as a Charter and both have turned out to be disasters. It would have been wiser to have backed off, but he did not. Now we are into this mess. He forced the patriation. Quebec did not sign. After six years of being out, the ten provincial premiers came together representing all three parties in the country and said: "We have to have the Constitution patriated. We have to get Quebec in to sign", because the business of the nation was being hampered. So, in 1986, all ten premiers agreed to have a round. That is what led to Meech Lake.
In Meech Lake, we had all four political parties, all premiers agreeing to it, and then it failed because of the opposition parties in a couple of provinces, as well as a weak Conservative government in Manitoba did not have the courage to stand up and speak for the nation. So we are into it, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to be able to comment on the Supreme Court of Canada and its decisions. The other thing Mr. Trudeau did in 1980 was to transfer massive power to the Supreme Court of Canada. The court, in a couple of

May 27, 1991
The Address
decisions on abortion, on Bill 101, have caused a malaise in the country. Formerly these matters were always settled by way of political adjustments and political compromise. But the court has the power to come down with a hard ruling and that has caused enormous malaise in this country. We are a long way from working it out.
I regret that my time has expired. I need at least 20 minutes to get through what I would like to say.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today on this final day of throne speech debate to put forward some of my comments and some of the comments from people in my constituency with reference to the plans of this government for the future and the plan that the government seems to have put in place for the past.
On the first page of the throne speech the words jump off the page:
This session will be a turning point in Canadian history.
There are many turning points and we are at a turning point in Canadian history. As I travel throughout my riding, as I travel across Canada into various provinces and territories, I find that there is a good deal of dismay at where this country has been taken over the last six and a half years, both socially, economically and politically.
It is interesting that in looking at our thrust toward unity of the country the Prime Minister would be so callous as he was the weekend before last, when he said that Canadians are not patriotic. Those types of comments simply are not helpful when we are trying to bridge the gap between Parliament and the ordinary Canadian voter. I object to that type of statement as do the people in my riding and I am sure across Canada.
One of my constituents, Mr. Jim Miltimore of Sum-merland, phoned me and I spoke to him again on the weekend. He vehemently opposed this. He and I feel proud to be Canadians. We are patriotic in our own way. We as Canadians are not necessarily demonstrative. We are not chest beaters. We are not flag wavers. We believe, or have up until now, in our country.
It is unfortunate that the Prime Minister, while talking of the turning point in Canadian history, talking about unity of the country, participation in prosperity, and a responsive government as he has in this throne speech,
at the same time he slaps the people of Canada with a comment like that. Those types of comments are not helpful.
I have spoken of the three main tenets of this throne speech, Canadian unity, participation in prosperity, and changing the way that Ottawa works-that is a responsive government. I want to speak first about Canadian unity and how the members of my community see some of this, and what I have seen in my participation in the finance committee, in the past public accounts committee, and in various travels across the country and throughout my riding.
Unity goes much further than simply talking about constitutional matters, it goes into economic and social well-being. If we look at some of the occurrences across Canada over the last few years, we have watched some of the things that people see as unifying forces being eroded. VIA Rail is an example. Sir John A. Macdonald made the agreement with CP Rail. The Canadian National Railway followed as a unifying force, making Canadians from coast to coast feel as if part of each other.
We have other modes of transportation. We have better highway systems, better air links, but the fact is that many of the small communities, rural Canadians, depend upon the railways, and railway service has been eroded. Our branch lines have been cut. Essentially the whole rail system has been lost in my riding alone. The Kettle Valley Rail Line has been abandoned and they are now in the process of taking it out. The section from Spences Bridge through the Okanagan, through Merritt and Princeton, have also been abandoned approximately a year ago and will soon no doubt be removed.
This is the type of thing that has unified Canada in the past, and with upgrading can unify Canada again. But they are not the only things. The attack on CBC radio and television by this government has been a terrible thing for rural Canada. In my riding alone I have had many petitions and letters of objection. People listen to the CBC for programs such as that hosted by Peter Gzowski, Cross Canada Checkup, Double Exposure. I can go on and name many radio programs listened to by many people in my area. CBC programs in all areas of Canada are always listened to and watched. A good
May 27, 1991

strong national television and radio network has a unifying effect upon Canada. That has been eroded.
Another matter which was debated in the House on Friday on a New Democratic motion is the funding of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. This is a major factor of unification within Canada. I would like to quote from a study and a submission made by the Union of British Columbia Municipalities to the government in summarizing the federal benefits of the RCMP.
I will quote directly from its fourth point: "The contribution to national unity is beyond dollars and cents.
What price does one put on the presence of the RCMP at our council inaugural meetings or the ever-present white and blue cars on our highways and streets?
It is incumbent on the federal government to sustain the image of national unity. In western Canada the RCMP provides policing and the federal government derives a great benefit to the national identity. The federal government is greatly underestimating the contribution of the RCMP to national unity in these negotiations."
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is a part of Canada's heritage. It is looked upon as a unifying factor by many people within Canada. The former Solicitor General proposed to substantially increase the cost to the extent where municipalities in my riding began talking about other options to RCMP.
It does not help to unify Canada when we erode some of the very systems that have brought this country together. Let me give some examples of the problems of passing on taxation from one level to the next level to the next level. Ultimately it comes out of the same pockets: the taxpayer's, the property owner's and the ordinary, middle and low income earner's.
In Penticton, with a population of approximately 25,500 people, the increase the former Solicitor General
The Address
has proposed, under the present system, would be almost $176,000 in increased policing costs for that community.
That passes on a major cost to the municipality. In Summerland, with a population of approximately 8,400 people, the cost is staggering: $72,663 extra under the new formula. In Merritt, also in my riding, with a population of approximately 6,100 people, the cost would be $118,831 in addition to what it is already paying.
The hon. member from Brant, the New Democratic Party Solicitor General critic, has written letters to the Solicitor General pointing out the importance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the unfairness of adding this extra tax burden to the local taxpayers and the major place that the RCMP takes in Canadian unity.
I implore this government to rethink the cost of policing and to rethink passing those costs on.
I would like to quote from a letter I received. It was a letter to the right hon. Prime Minister from Mr. R. J. Shewfelt, the mayor of the municipality of Summerland. Let me quote two sections of that letter to point out the feeling in our area toward the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and toward the anticipated increases in cost. The mayor says:
-we are- a level of government picking our tax dollars from the same tree, the taxpayer, and we find the shifting of responsibility to this degree completely unacceptable and unthinkable. We beseech you to please rethink your application to this agreement as we find it absolutely deplorable.
Mayor Shewfelt goes on to say:
If this action were to come to fulfilment, it would only further alienate the west and we feel this is a very real danger. We feel the west is a trading partner, and surely, we are entitled to the same consideration being given to the third world countries to develop and implement trade.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is a real part of British Columbia, a real part of national unity. We in our communities in the Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt riding want it to remain as the main area of law enforcement in our area.
Let me move on to another area. The government has spoken in the Speech from the Throne about more funding for education, et cetera. What we have seen in

The Address
Bill C-69 and in the last budget is the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan and the cap on Established Programs Financing.
It is interesting that some of this is just getting out into the various ridings and they are coming to realize that once again it appears to those in the west and to those in the east, those who are being hit by bills such as Bill C-69, that we are being treated differently. We are being discriminated against for the fact that we live out of the golden triangle of the east. The capping of those funds is because right now we happen to be doing reasonably well economically in comparison, for instance, to Ontario throughout this recession.
Let there be no mistake. There are problems and there are many bankruptcies, but people are realizing that the tax burden is simply being shifted down. Although perhaps the taxes will remain the same at the federal level and they may even remain the same at the provincial level, the municipalities must balance their budgets. In balancing their budgets, they have to come up with the tax money to cover these various expenditures. Taxes are passed on to the property owner who lives in the municipality.
The boundary country has some 200 signatures attached to a letter from Mrs. Thelma Drinkwater of Greenwood, British Columbia. I would like to quote this letter, recently received by my office. It says:
Please find enclosed a petition signed by more than two hundred voters. We protest the passing of Bill C-69. Our taxpayers are already paying out more of their income than they can afford to cover the cost of the Social Services Programs. If we do not receive our fair share of Federal support it will either mean a raise in taxes or a cutback in this service.
Neither of these options are acceptable. We therefore plead with you to make our feelings known on (this) subject.
I speak out, as I have on Bill C-69, to point out to this House that here are 200 people from areas such as Greenwood, Grand Forks and Midway who are speaking out through me in objection to the passing on of taxes to property owners in these areas.
Another thing that unifies this country and assists rural Canada is our telephone system. Before the CRTC right now is an application by Unitel to break down what is known as a monopoly. It may be thought that it is a little bit unusual for someone from the New Democratic Party to speak out for a monopoly. In this case it is very clear that if we deregulate to the extent that Unitel
wishes or let Unitel in on the long distance telephone responses, we are going to run into major problems, problems that certainly Unitel does not want to talk about.
Right now we all know that there is a subsidy of somewhere between $23 and $39 a month for local telephone services. We also get though this our telephones installed for a very limited prices and all of our servicing done for nothing. We do not pay for our local telephone calls. This is at the expense to some extent of greater long distance rates; a way of equalizing, if you will, the difficulties that rural communities have in communicating with each other.
If we allow Unitel to break in to the lucrative long distance market and drop those prices, we are going to see what happened in the United States seven years ago when the cost of local telephone service will go up substantially on every one of our bills. Those people now in the lower income levels who barely get by on the little amount of income they have will no longer be able to afford the luxury of a telephone. Telephones are so essential in keeping in contact with each other in rural communities and so essential for emergency services in rural communities where transportation of a public nature is unheard of. I am worried about this sort of thing happening.
Mr. Speaker, you have indicated that my time is up. My understanding is that I had 20 minutes of time. I still have two minutes of time. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Canada Post in the rural areas has to be built up and it is being broken down.
Let me move on briefly to the area of participating in prosperity.
Some of the other members have referred to crossborder shopping and the difficulty for the small business community. We cannot knock people for wanting to get the best value for their dollar.
Right now, they see a problem with what is occurring in Canada. They want to get the best value for their dollar, but they are also protesting the high taxes they see as a problem in this country. The GST, the high interest rates, the high dollar and, to some extent, the free trade agreement all have something to do with people going across the border and buying their goods.
May 27, 1991

It is interesting to look at the free trade agreement as it affects communities such as Osoyoos where I live. Right on the border in Osoyoos, one of the local retailers there, Super Value Store number 36 owner Keith Sheardown, has written me a letter in which he sets out the problems he has just in the area of milk, cheese and what not.
He points out that a Super Value store some 30 miles further from the border is able to sell its milk at a substantially higher price than he does.
While he charges $4.45 for a four-litre jug of milk, across the border that same jug of milk is $1.99. He cannot sell the milk at the same price and this causes problems. It costs jobs and bankruptcies. We are certainly seeing an increase in the number of bankruptcies in Canada and in British Columbia, partially caused by the problem of cross-border shopping.
The throne speech sets out so many things in such glowing terms, but if we look at the history of this government and if we look at what is happening to Canada under this government, it is deplorable. I have one word for this throne speech as a result of that history. That word is: "hypocrisy".

It is interesting. Somebody on the weekend from his riding spoke to me about the CBC and felt it was absolutely ludicrous that as a government we are continuing to subsidize this national network to the tune of $1.4 billion.

They agree that this is a good function to perform in Canada, but is it necessary to subsidize it at that level?
In fact his constituents are encouraging me, and I am sure him as well, to try to retain the value and the benefits of CBC, but to continue to cut the deficit and our subsidies to it.
The same message could be had for the others. One area on which I have to stand firm with my colleague from the Okanagan is his concern for the potential problems for rural Canada as a result of the possible breakdown of the current monopoly situation regarding communication.
I can see as a former businessman the potential for competition by not only businesses but people who live in the ribbon across Canada where 95 per cent of Canadians live.
For rural Canada, it will create a real problem. My question to the hon. member is this: Does he, through his thinking and dealing with this problem, have any potential solution? If Unitel is successful, is there some way that the people in the rural areas of his riding and mine could continue to receive the assistance and the assurance of service that they do now under the existing monopoly system?

I will deal with the Unitel situation first of all. As I understand it, in British Columbia B.C. Tel, although objecting to UnitePs application, at the same time has put in an application to the CRTC to be able to charge those various rates. That is my understanding. I

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my good friend from Okanagan-Similkameen- Merritt and it is with respect to the Kettle Valley. I have often wondered, being from Lethbridge, why Kettle Valley was closed down many years ago, because it seems to be a more direct route to the coast.
I am wondering if he might comment on that. I know it was cut by the previous government and that was many, many years ago.
With respect to the RCMP, the people who have approached me are always surprised when I give them some additional information. For example, when they find out that the federal government is paying 25 per cent of the RCMP costs, I say to them: "Why should that be? When the Quebec Provincial Police are funded entirely by the Quebec taxpayer and the Ontario Provincial Police are paid for entirely by the Ontario taxpayer, why should the people in those two provinces pay extra taxes to cover the RCMP who are, in effect, the provincial police force in our respective provinces?" When they see it from that point of view, they often admit: "It is true. They should not be paying for it. We should pay more to handle our own policing."
As for the CBC, when we came to power it was getting $800 million. Today it is $1.4 billion. That is an absolute increase of enormous proportions. It is cutting back for the same reason other media outlets are having to cut back, because there is less advertising as a result of the recession. Why should the taxpayers make up that difference, rather than the CBC having to cut as the other media outlets have had to do?

First of all, I will deal with the specious argument that Quebec and Ontario are not benefiting. If we look at where forces are placed, although we are getting municipal forces in, say, British Columbia, in Ontario and in Quebec we have the Canadian Law
Enforcement Unit, CLEU, which deals on a broader basis with drug law enforcement and major crime enforcement across Canada. We have many benefits accruing to both Quebec and to Ontario as a result of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In 1951, for instance, British Columbia had a provincial police force. As a result of the unity question, to some extent because of the idea that bigger is better and the new technologies that had to be kept up with, it was felt in British Columbia at that time that the better route to go was to dismantle the provincial police and go with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
As we have seen in some major investigations, it has probably proven to be somewhat of a good move, especially when we watch the various municipal or provincial police forces keeping information in an investigation to themselves instead of sharing it resulting in two or three ongoing investigations. There is a definite benefit to all communities and to Canada as a whole from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Let me move on to the CBC argument. In Canada, as a young nation, we have something that I think the members opposite are ignoring to some extent, and that is the cultural aspect of Canada. We are a young country, 124 years old. Our subsidies to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation gave opportunities to programs like Tommy Hunter and Don Messer in the maritimes. People such as Anne Murray received their big break on CBC. If it was not for groups like this and symphony orchestras, for instance, presenting major productions on the CBC, we would not be as far ahead right now in Canada culturally. It services that which is not served by the private sector.
I am sure my friend from Cariboo-Chilcotin was probably talking to a broadcaster about this.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to speak through you to my constituents and Canadians on what our Prime Minister has presented in the Speech from the Throne.
I understand that I immediately follow our colleagues from the NDP and that there are ideological positions that seem fairly firm to us. They seem to be saying and do say that the Speech from the Throne is a rehash and presents nothing for immediate action. If we really look at the Throne Speech, and I believe I do not do so in a partisan or aggressive way, we realize that before finding the recipe, we must again identify some ingredients and especially the pillars on which a society that is developing extremely rapidly must build its future-and the future is now.
Coming back to the Speech from the Throne, we see three basic points in it. Therefore the government's plan is in three clearly identified parts. First comes unity. As we say in the Speech from the Throne, a united country is the best guarantee for the survival of our way of life. Psychology, sociology and a knowledge of society and nature are the basis for this statement. There is no doubt that to have diversity, common projects are necessary and unity must be a prime consideration. Without unity, there is chaos. The government therefore wanted to put first and foremost this basic concept of national unity, a united country, and to do so, as other speakers have said, the government will set up some committees that are necessary, not superfluous, to determine more precisely the pith and essence, the thinking, needs and dynamics of individuals and the population as a whole.
The second part, as was said, deals with prosperity. For an organization to prosper, it must have unity of thought, action and direction, as teachers of management know. Prosperity is a result of this unified approach. The government is not afraid to say that it wants this prosperity under certain conditions and identifies very specific objectives: participation in the creation of 2.5 million new jobs. This is a concrete goal, a goal that can be reached since the Conservative government, from

May 27, 1991
The Address
1984 on, has been constantly faced with goals difficult to attain, but identifiable, identified and reachable.
So, 2.5 million new jobs and an increase of at least 25 per cent in real income by year 2000 are a necessity. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 13, 1991, the government formalized the major national concerns of the Canadian people and outlined what the main themes of the federal legislation and administration will be for the next few years. In view of the present constitutional concerns of the Canadians, it was normal to define this constitutional context in the Speech from the Throne. But we also know that, as important as national soul-searching might be, it will never prevail over quality of life, the preservation of our social programs and the protection of our environment in the eyes of the Canadians, all of which depends on the productivity of our capital and human resources. The Speech from the Throne, of May 13, 1991 stated:
Increasing economic prosperity is first and foremost an issue of
people.
We are entering the age of knowledge and how well Canadians live will depend on how well they learn. To face this particular challenge, the government announced the forthcoming release of a work paper on education.
The federal government is wondering if the $11 billion it spends every year on education is well spent. The results are not convincing: "Three out of ten students drop-out of high school before graduating. Four out of ten adults cannot read or do math well enough to perform everyday tasks."
Included in the Speech from the Throne are the following education goals for the year 2000: cutting illiteracy rates in half; ensuring that ninety percent of Canadians attain high school diplomas or the equivalent by age twenty-five; doubling the number of post-secon-

May 27, 1991
The Address
dary graduates in mathematics, the sciences and engineering; and quadrupling the training provided by employers to their employees.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should find innovative means to help us achieve those goals, at a minimal cost. In Canada, education is financed by the school boards with property taxes, and by the federal and provincial governments, mainly through taxation and loans.
Consequently, almost $11 billion are transferred from the federal to the provincial governments, where those $11 billion are eaten up by various provincial bureaucracies, major education institutions, universities, school boards, et cetera.
All those institutions try to anticipate our collective education needs, that is the number of students opting either for humanities or sciences, the number of elementary schools, the number of colleges and universities, the various services provided to students, the curriculum, the option systems, the credit systems, students' preferences and the demand.
At one end of this planning pyramid, you will find schoolchildren and students who often have to attend schools not of their own choosing, travel by more or less adequate means, and specialize in hard-to-define areas because of the very large number of options available. Too often, the only reason students stay in school is to meet the criteria set by the experts and in the end, get a diploma in whatever subject, also certified by the experts.
Mr. Speaker, I think our education system has lost its focus which should be our students. Our education system does not realize that we live in a market economy. To change the system, the bureaucracy will have to give way to the laws of supply and demand, and to achieve this, all levels of government will have to change their funding programs for education.
Instead of letting public funds, as so often happens, serve the interests of huge bureaucracies, they should be channeled directly to the beneficiaries, in other words, the students.
Governments will have to start implementing a system that provides students with study qualification certificates.
With these certificates, students will be able to choose their subjects, schools, teachers, and so forth. The qualification certificate system could initially show a preference for science and engineering, since those are the areas where the need is greatest and where we have the most catching up to do. The system will encourage private and public educational institutions to compete and also give those institutions an incentive to be more market-and efficiency-oriented. This system would also be a major incentive for the big bad unions, which, unfortunately, are often so concerned about the vested rights of their members that they tend to overlook the needs of young people and the labour market.
The qualification certificate system would do away with a burdensome bureaucracy that has not always proved to be worthwhile. Transfers to lower levels of government must be replaced with transfers to the users themselves.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians must be able to make their own decisions on their future. It no longer makes sense to have bureaucrats decide what careers our young people will choose and how they will prepare for those careers.
In fact, President George Bush recently suggested that U.S. federal funds for education be made directly available to the parents of young Americans, so it would be up to parents and their children to choose their schools or other educational institutions.
Mr. Speaker, in our discussions on educational reform, we should take a look at some examples on the other side of the border. The city of Milwaukee, in Wisconsin, has made qualification certificates available to enable its young people to choose the schools where they want to study.
Similar programs have been implemented in Iowa, Arkansas, Utah, Ohio and so forth.
Mr. Speaker, this concept of channeling transfer payments to young students will form the nucleus of my representations to those who govern this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as members of Parliament begin the third session of
May 27, 1991

Parliament, it is appropriate to look back over the last two and a half years since I was elected to serve the Cardigan riding.
In the period of time since I was elected, I have learned many things and I have met many people. The most important thing I have learned is that serving the hard working people of eastern Prince Edward Island is one of the best jobs I could have.
I thank the people of Cardigan for the trust and respect they have placed in me. As I listened to the Speech from the Thone, one thing kept entering my mind, and that was the government record. For my constituents, the people of Prince Edward Island, it is difficult to find much good in the record over the last seven years.
While this government has presided over the six best years of economic growth, the disparity between Atlantic Canada and the rest of the country has grown. While the economy was booming in central Canada, the fishery was failing. While the government was talking about jobs, jobs, jobs, it was jobs leaving Prince Edward Island. An example is the closure of the CFB in Summerside.
This government has had six years of expanding revenue and still has failed to control the deficit. In all fairness, the record of the government is bad. With a record like this behind it, it is hard to believe any of the vague promises in the throne speech.
Much of the throne speech is concentrated on the constitutional crisis that we are now facing. I would like to make perfectly clear that Quebec was not left out in the cold when the Constitution was brought home in 1982. Quebec was led by Rene Levesque, a man who was dedicated to Quebec's separation. Then Prime Minister Trudeau could have offered Levesque the moon and the stars and he would not have signed. Only one thing would have been acceptable to the PQ government in 1982, and that was Quebec's separation.
The situation grew worse when the Meech Lake Accord died last summer. I will not get into the argument of whether Meech Lake was good or bad. Today that is not important. What is important is why the accord failed.
The Address
The one person responsible for the failure of Meech lake was the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister pushed and pushed until people were backed into a corner. Most people react negatively when pushed into a corner. With his famous "roll the dice" comment, the Prime Minister destroyed much of the goodwill in the nation.
The decision now is: Where do we go from here? We in the Liberal Party do not want to play politics with the country. That is why we support the principle of a new constitutional committee to evaluate the concrete constitutional proposals. However, we disagree strongly with the timetable the government is trying to impose.
The new committee is to start work in September and is to complete work by January 1992. The framework is simply too short. Because the committee is to develop the government's negotiating position, it will just leave a few short months before the proposed Quebec referendum.
The Prime Minister is painting the country into another comer where he could roll the dice again and lose again. To avoid that situation, the government should put its cards on the table by June 1 and have the committee start working thereafter. Anything that would save time certainly should be considered.
I would like to share with you, Mr. Speaker, what I think should go into a renewed Constitution. Any constitutional change should reflect the importance of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. All Canadians have a strong attachment to the charter. The preservation of our fundamental freedoms is supreme, and no amendment to the Constitution should change that.
We should also look at writing an inspiring statement of the nature of Canada. The statement should outline all those things that make Canada the best country in the world. It should state the values that we share, commitment to our two official languages, recognition of our diverse cultural heritage, recognition of the distinctiveness of Quebec society and recognition of the role of the aboriginal people.
When the Fathers of Confederation wrote the Constitution of Canada in 1867, they divided the powers, giving to each level of government the powers they felt appropriate. What was appropriate in 1867 may no longer be

May 27, 1991
appropriate today. After all, the world has changed a lot in 124 years.
The fundamental principle must be that the power should rest with the level of government that can handled the matter best. The focus should be what is best for the people, not governments, bureaucrats or politicians. In many areas the federal and provincial governments could co-operate. An example is the environment. The federal government should be able to set up guideline legislation stating national standards, leaving it up to the provinces to adapt these national standards to regional and provincial realities.
Historically the federal government has used its spending powers to enter into areas of provincial responsibility. The problem in the past has been how to reconcile the limitations of the spending power with the needs of national standards.
With a change in the division of powers, it becomes possible to achieve a constitutional limitation of the federal spending power without compromising national standards.
Over the last year much attention has been paid to the problems facing Canada's aboriginal people. There is a broad consensus and understanding in Canada of the need to deal with their status, rights and claims. A constitutional reform package must enshrine the rights of the aboriginal people to self-government.
As it stands right now, most areas of the Constitution can be amended with the 7-50 formula, with seven provinces and 50 per cent of the population. However, for many Canadians this is not acceptable. A new amending formula should recognize the basic equalities of the regions of the west, Quebec, Ontario and Atlantic Canada. Each region should have a veto on any constitutional changes that are not in the interests of the people living there.
These are the things I would like to see in our new Canadian Constitution. The stumbling block is our attitude, because in many ways we are our own worst enemies. Canadians are often too harsh on themselves and other Canadians, and that has to change. Far too often we get caught up in the small problems of life. We get caught up in the rat race of life and do not take time to consider how good we have it here in Canada.
With all our problems, and there are many, it is difficult to look under the grey tarnish at the sparkling silver underneath. It is often said that Canadians envy Americans because they are so patriotic and proud to be Americans. The time has come for each and every one of us to say that we are proud to be Canadians. I am proud to be a Canadian.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several weeks ago I rose in this Chamber to participate in the debate on the proposed changes to the rules of the House. In that speech, I pointed out that there is a breakdown in our parliamentary system.
The Address
I also attempted to show the principles behind our parliamentary system and how important it is that members of the government recognize those principles in order for our democracy to work.
My comments have clearly fallen on deaf ears. Today I rise to participate in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne is the cause of summons. Simply stated, members of Parliament are summoned here to Ottawa to consider legislation and taxation which the cabinet claims it needs in order to govern. Our mandate as elected members is clear. We have been sent here to Parliament to represent our constituents' interests when we consider the cabinet's requests.
The reason there is such ceremony surrounding the cabinet's request is to symbolize for all Canadians-including ourselves, members of the other place, and ministers of the Crown-the supremacy of the legislature over the executive branch.
On Monday, May 13, we heard several reasons why we were summoned here to Ottawa. One of those reasons was to consider proposals from the cabinet to once again change the way we operate in this Chamber and I quote:
My government will propose further reform so that all Members of Parliament can better fulfil their obligations to their constituents.
What right does the executive branch have to interfere in the operations of this Chamber?
Another of the reasons we were summoned to Ottawa was for the cabinet to inform us that it intended to establish a parliamentary committee to study the proposal to amend the Constitution.
This committee will, according to the Speech from the Throne:
Havel in order to hear the views of men and women across Canada. In each jurisdiction it visits, the committee will be mandated to meet in public session with its counterpart provincial or territorial legislative committee or, where no such committee exists, with counterpart legislators.
How could the cabinet announce that we will be establishing another committee when the original committee has not yet even reported? I do not ask this question to be facetious. The Speech from the Throne said:

May 27, 1991
The Address
The respect of the people for a Parliament and for Parliamentarians
is essential for a healthy democracy. But the appearance, and
sometimes the reality, of excessive party discipline-
-among other things, has-
-eroded that respect in Canada.
The only way the cabinet could have included it in its Speech from the Throne and announced that there will be a committee of Parliament is if it intends to use party discipline to force us to establish it. The hypocrisy of it all.
I would remind the government once again that the committee to amend the Constitution has not yet reported. There is an inherent flaw in logic for the government to pre-empt the work of one parliamentary committee on the grounds that it believes the work of parliamentary committees to be essential. If it respects parliamentary committees, it should be waiting for this committee to recommend how to proceed. If it has no respect for the parliamentary committees, then it should not use them as a mechanism to amend the Constitution.
On May 13 we heard more of the reasons why we were summoned to Ottawa. The cabinet wishes us to consider legislation that it believes will improve unity, prosperity and government responsiveness. On Tuesday the hon. Leader of the Opposition pointed out that the government's policies in the last seven years have resulted in the unequivocal loss of the Canadian public's confidence in the government's ability to run this country effectively-
I agree with the Canadian public and with the Leader of the Official Opposition. However, it is important that the people of Canada realize that it is not the political system that has failed them but the Conservative government that has failed them. Why should the Canadian people believe anything this government proposes in this next session?
The truth is that this government has not honoured the public trust which empowered it to form a government. It has not provided effective legislation. It is time for this government to take some real initiative. This government is a non-committal government. It is not committed to its social policies. It is not committed to its environmental policies. It is not even committed to Canadian unity.
How can we possibly believe that the government is, in any way, committed to the Canadian public.
The cabinet's agenda of some weeks ago confirmed this government's lack of commitment to the Canadian public. It confirmed this government's lack of substance and it confirmed the lack of any effective plan to launch Canada into the 21st century.
The only thing this government is committed to is double digit unemployment, the GST and economic disparity.
I remind the House that at a time when it is imperative for Canada to increase its competitiveness in the world economy, funds have been slashed for education, training and research and development. The very foundations of our economic competitiveness and prosperity are being deliberately and systematically eroded.
Further, while the government eloquently espouses its vision of restructuring the economy, the only vision this government is providing Canadians, after seven years of economic brutality, is that of workers standing on street corners or in unemployment lines. The government has not provided programs to deal with the impact of the free trade agreement. The government has not provided relief for the 1.4 million unemployed Canadians. Nor has the government protected low income Canadians from the GST.
What the government has provided is the first ever made-in-Canada recession, record bankruptcies and government policies directly responsible for an increased deficit. A strong economy is the basis for a united country.
I do not understand how this government can put this country's constitutional crisis on hold again. Why is this government waiting for another committee report? I would suggest that the government is stalling for more time.
They have tried unsuccessfully in the past to resolve these matters. Why would Canadians have confidence in the record of these successive failures? We must solve the constitutional problems immediately so we can move on to the other problems this government has created.
One more item in the throne speech was a commitment to reduce trade barriers between provinces, something that this government has talked about for years now, and still no real solutions have been developed. How can this government be concerned with interprovincial trade when every initiative it has taken since its

initial election has worked against that goal? In 1988, it finalized the free trade agreement with the United States. The free trade agreement works against the concept of cross-Canadian interprovincial trade.
This government talks about education, but how can the government expect provinces to pay for the education cost, to pay for regional development, to reduce illiteracy and to reduce the number of unemployed when it systematically cuts transfer payments? How can we educate with no money? How can we create jobs when every day more and more people become unemployed directly as a result of this government's untenable employment policies.
If there is a lack of productivity in this country, it is due to cutbacks in research and development, cutbacks in transfer payments, cutbacks in education funding and cutbacks in retraining and training programs. How can the government demand Canadian workers to increase its productivity when it ties the hands of these workers behind their backs?
If I may quote from Senator Hubert Humphrey's last speech in 1977, he said:
The moral test of government is how it treats those who are in the
dawn of life, the children; those who are in the twilight of life, the
aged; and those who are in the shadows of life, the sick, the needy and
the handicapped.
How can this government believe it has the moral wherewithal to govern?
The Speech from the Throne spoke of non-partisanship as essential for Parliament to operate. The Prime Minister asks that the opposition recognize its dual role as partisan politicians and parliamentarians.
I would suggest in closing that if the Prime Minister would recognize his dual roles as an elected member of Parliament and as an appointed head of the executive branch, his government would be well on its way to achieving unity, prosperity and government responsiveness.

speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Jonquiere has the floor for 10 minutes.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I appreciate having this opportunity to take part today in the debate on the recent Speech from the Throne. It probably was the most important in modern Canadian history, as it deals with three absolutely fundamental issues.
These are national unity, prosperity and government efficiency. I believe it is the most important made in Canada in the twentieth century because, as we know, Canada could well split up in the next 18 months if no solution is found to settle the national unity issue.
Since the Constitution was patriated in 1982, Quebec has been excluded from the present Constitution and has refused to participate in any constitutional conference, even more so considering the outcome of the last attempt, with the Meech initiative.
So, Quebec, more than ever, feels cornered and is not participating in any conference, hence the potential for a split within 18 months. I mentionned I was happy to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, because, while my government and our Prime Minister were preparing the Speech from the Throne, my colleagues on the Beau-doin-Edwards Committee and myself were travelling all over the country in an attempt to find a way out of the present constitutional deadlock.
As a matter of fact, we have a four-point mandate to answer the following questions: Should we or should we not hold a referendum? Does the existing constitutional amending formula meet our needs? Should it be changed and, if so, what should it be? Finally, should a constituent assembly be set up to solve our constitutional problems? Add to that the issue of public participation. Let us not forget that Canadians do not want a rerun of what they have seen on television during the Meech episode, with individuals making decisions behind closed doors on what the Constitution of Canada should be. Now, the Canadian people want to take part in the process.
May 27, 1991

So, the importance of the Speech from the Throne is clear in relation to national unity which is linked to prosperity. Constitutional problems of course cannot help this country's economic situation. We can see what is happening with the unemployment level still climbing.
I don't think anyone likes the economic situation we are in and we must strive to find ways to bring that level down, to ensure that more jobs and opportunities are available to the Canadians people.
That being said, I would also like to talk about prosperity, Mr. Speaker. We have set targets. By the year 2000, we want to have created 2,5 million new jobs. We are also going to try and raise the real incomes of Canadians by 25 percent. But all that is linked to the issue of Canadian unity. Unless we come up with an answer within the next 18 months, nothing will do. On the contrary, times will be tough for Quebec and all of Canada.
The Speech from the Throne also mentions an important subject, education; our government talks about national objectives for education. That startles many people, since education is under provincial jurisdiction, especially in Quebec. But basically, in the present debate, the whole question of power sharing under the Constitution must be reviewed. Is it good and desirable for Canada to set national standards and ask the provinces to apply them in accordance with their own particular characteristics? Let us take health as an example. The central government sets standards and objectives for health and tells the provinces to apply them on the basis of their needs. Quebec has its own health care system of which it is proud.
Of course, gradually things must change. We must evolve on the basis of our society's present needs. Quebec wants some changes. Should national health standards be reviewed and updated? Why not?
The same thing applies to education. Ideally, instead of each province setting its own standards in a disconnected way from the others, is it not time to think that it might be much better if we had national standards for education?
We talk about free trade and economic exchanges among the provinces and section 6(2)(a) of the Constitution says that all Canadians can settle in any province of the country. If your child leaves a province with its own education system and goes to another province where
The Address
things are completely different and there are no national standards and no unity in all this, is that good or should we not review this thoroughly to see how it could be changed? But the federal government must not say, "This is the true standard and how we will apply it." It must not be done unilaterally but in cooperation with the provincial ministers and coordinated with them. They together should consider what national standards we should have. Furthermore, these standards should be reviewed periodically because it is no use having standards, an unreachable ideal, if the provinces do not have the money they need to reach those standards.
So when we talk about constitutional reform, with the coming changes, we must review all that.
Mr. Speaker, I still think that Quebec will be part of the next Constitution-and I am sure there will be a new one. It will not be perfect, but if we manage to change the amending formula in order to get rid of the unanimity rule, then, even flawed, our new Constitution would at least enable us to make future changes.
I would like to make an important point, Mr. Speaker, because I heard some of my colleagues talk about equalization. I happened to read in Le Reveil, a local newspaper from my constituency of Jonquiere, an editorial written by Mr. Marcel Martel, who was saying: "Per capita, the Tories give out $548 to Quebec and $1,652 to Newfoundland. Thanks to his Conservative buddies, Clyde Wells must be having a good laugh. Try to figure this one out."
Mr. Speaker, that shows how people do not understand how transfer payments work. There are three kinds of transfer payments: the Established Programs Financing, the equalization payments, and the Canada Assistance Plan.
What is the Established Programs Financing? It is funding given to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education among other things. In 1991-1992, the Established Programs Financing totalled $20 billion, of which $5 billion went to Quebec. Equalization payments are the second most important type of transfer payments to the provinces. Out of $8 billion given out in equalization, Quebec received $3.8 billion, and Newfoundland $938 million. That is what we mean, Mr. Speaker, when we say figures can be misleading. To

May 27, 1991
The Address
say Quebec receive only $548 per capita, while Newfoundland get $1,652 is like saying Quebec is not getting any subsidy. Now, wait just a moment! Newfoundland has a population of 560,000 people; if you multiply
560,000	by $1,652 and then 6.6 million by $548, you will see that Quebec is receiving a lot more than Newfoundland. You have to be cautious when you use these figures.
Quebec is among the provinces receiving more equalization payments than others. In fact, three provinces get no equalization payment at all, Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario. Other provinces receive payments because they are not as prosperous. That is called equalization. Rich provinces pay for poorer ones. It could very well be that 30 years from now, Newfoundland, thanks to an extraordinary find, will contribute more for British Columbia or Quebec. That is the way our country works. Rich provinces should contribute to help poorer provinces. That is nothing to be sad about. It is the very basis of our country and of equalization.
Mr. Speaker, this is an important Speech from the Throne with three themes: unity, prosperity and government responsiveness. Those are three essential issues. We have to find a way out of the constitutional impasse in the next 18 months.
Our Beaudoin-Edwards committee will report to this House by the beginning of July and other committees will try and solve the problems of Senate reform, division of powers and aboriginal rights.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Questions and comments for a five minutes period. The hon. member for St. Boniface.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the comments made by my hon. colleague with whom I sit on the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee and with whom I worked a lot and expect to work even harder in the next few days.
He mentioned, if I understood him well, that Canadian unity had an economic dimension. Personally, I believe it. Without "economic harmony" across this country, can we have unity? I do not think so, and that is more or less what my colleague from my party just said.
But the question I want to ask, and I do not mmention it out of spite, is why this government, for example, might allow CP Rail to reroute its trains through the
United States? It seems to me that could entail possible job losses for Manitoba, for Winnipeg, Brandon and other Western provinces. Allowing such a move, to my mind, would worsen the economic situation and tear the country apart even further, and destroy the bonds already established. That was my first question.
Now a second one. He talked about national objectives, and I really appreciated his remarks, because I believe that we can have national objectives provided they are set in a cooperative way. They should not be imposed by a level on another one; I believe that we have to work together in order to improve the economic situation, national unity, etc.
Does he believe that a new federalism would be fundamentally based on the principle of cooperation?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the first comment or question of my hon. colleague, I would like to remind him that, in the last few years, the government has endeavoured to expand our market in the world.
Canada cannot do business only within its borders, since it exports 30 per cent of its production. Trade between Canada and the United States is a $200 billion a year business. If we look at the provinces, Ontario's exports to Quebec, for instance, total $21 billion annually, whereas Quebec exports to Ontario amount to $17.9 billion.
In that context, and that also applies to our Crown corporations in the transport industry, we must look to foreign markets, among which is our closest partner, the United States, and Mexico, with whom we are working on a free trade agreement.
Moreover, one must not forget that, as of next December, we will have to compete with an economic union composed of 12 European countries. We will then have to face international competition.
That also explains why it is important, in the field of education, that Canada improve its record as regards technology. We are presently not performing well enough in that field and there is room for improvement. The same is true in the field of education, of course, since those two fields are directly related.
What will be the outcome of the next constitutional conference? What will be the powers of Quebec? Will the situation be completely different? It is too early to tell; nobody knows yet, but it is clear that federalism
May 27, 1991

The Address
must be changed and renewed. Yesterday, I was pleased to see your leader, Mr. Chretien, say that Quebec should have a right of veto. This is an issue that our committee has discussed on numerous occasions, namely that Quebec should have a form of protection enshrined in the next Constitution.
That being said, let's wait and see. First, there is the report that will be tabled by our Beaudoin-Edwards Committee, and then the Spicer Commission report will be tabled by July 1st. There is another joint commission of members and senators, that will travel across the country and meet their provincial counterparts. Following that, the government will be in a position to put forward a new constitutional proposal aimed at making sure that Quebec can again be part of the Canadian family and prosper within that context.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Terrebonne.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am very pleased to have this opportunity today to take part in the debate on the Speech from the Throne.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to share some thoughts with my colleagues regarding the intention expressed by my government in the Speech from the Throne to set national goals in education.
If I get into this subject, Mr. Speaker, it is because it appears to have been misunderstood by some members of this House. You know, over the last few days, we have heard some members of this House complain about interference. Others hide behind the curtains, Mr. Speaker. Why? Because the government wants our young people to have access some day to a lucrative and rewarding job. And why, Mr. Speaker? Because this government wants to give future generations of Quebecers and Canadians, men and women, an opportunity to enjoy an even better quality of life.
Why do members hide behind the curtains and shout "murder"? Because our government reacts when our country is about to miss the turn towards an increasingly competitive global economy.
Mr. Speaker, they shout "murder" and they hide behind the curtains. It may be the best way for them to avoid speaking on the issue when they have nothing sensible to say. But, nevertheless, there are facts that deserve that we go beyond partisan politics.
Thirty per cent of our students drop out of high school before graduating. Is that acceptable? No, it is not acceptable. Should we remain silent when the demographers predict that Canada will soon be a country with hardly no manpower? Should we keep doing nothing when we know that half of all the jobs that will be created between 1990 and 1999 will require more than five years of training after high school? Should we close our eyes on the fact that today, only 60 per cent of our workers graduate from high school?
Mr. Speaker, should we not at least react when we learn that Canadian employers spend half of what our neighbours to the South spend for the training of their employees, and eight times less than what the Germans spend? Should we give up all of our responsibilities because we know that our future prosperity depends on the knowledge and the skills that Canadian men and women will have acquired? Should we keep our eyes closed? No. The world and the global economy are going through a phase of radical change. Borders are opening up. Economical and political blocks are emerging. Competition is constantly increasing. We cannot afford to miss the train. We must adapt. We must train our manpower. We must prepare our workers for the future. That is the challenge we have to face and that is what is proposed in the Speech from the Throne.
Quebec found its identity in the early sixties. At that time, Quebecers really took their destiny into their hands. That is the period that was, and still is, called the Quiet Revolution. That revolution that put Quebec on the way of a new prosperity didn't come about by itself. Around the same time, the Parent Report led to a reform of the Quebec education system. That is almost 30 years ago.
Today, when a revolution is already under way in the world economy, it seems more and more that results achieved in education will be clearly insufficient to guarantee all Canadians a prosperous future. To benefit

May 27, 1991
The Address
from this revolution, we must go back to the drawing board, rethink our approach to education and, instead of missing the whole point, we must discuss the question together and find solutions to the problem.
In spite of all this, Mr. Speaker, there are still members in this House who are opposed to the fact the government wants to prepare Canadian men and women to face the challenges of year 2000. For what reason? Because they say that education is a provincial responsibility. But we have always recognized this and we still do. It is written in black and white in the Speech from the Throne and I quote:
My government recognizes that education is a provincial
responsibility under the Constitution and respects that fact.
I think it is very clear, Mr. Speaker. The Premier of Quebec himself, who strongly defends Quebecers' interests, said, and I quote:
We must discuss some form of cooperation for common goals. We
do not see why we should refuse to discuss.
Mr. Speaker, after the Meech Lake failure, the Premier of Quebec stated that his province would have discussions with Ottawa only if Quebec's interests were directly concerned. I believe this is the case.
Quebec is an integral part of the Canadian economic union. It largely benefits from its trade with other provinces since it sells more goods and services in Canada than on foreign markets. It's by opting freely for the federal system, while asserting our distinct identity, that we were able to create our prosperity. That is a system where the provinces are sovereign in their respective jurisdictions, but in which all Canadians have their say on matters which concern the entire country.
Besides, the Belanger-Campeau Commission Report, that some hon. members in this House should read entirely, states with good reason that: "Federalism, as a political organization principle, is characterized by the flexibility of the arrangements and structures that it makes possible".
So, Mr. Speaker, this government always believed in recognizing the regional diversity of the country. By meeting the demands of Quebec in the Meech Lake Accord, this government was recognizing, not only the distinct identity of Quebec, but also the right of the provinces to opt out of national programs, with compensation, when they thought they could administer more
effectively these programs. That was the spirit of the Meech Lake Accord and it is still implicit on this government's actions. So, the discussions that this government will have with the provinces as far as education and training are concerned, will be consistent with this spirit.
Since 1984, our government has taken a lot of initiatives to prepare Canada for the challenges of the year 2000. When we came to power in 1984, you will recall that our country was dangerously mismanaged and heavily in debt. We have not taken the easy way out and we have put in place tools to garantee our prosperity.
A more responsible management allowed us to slow down the growth of deficit. The Free Trade Agreement, taxation reform, privatization initiatives, government spending cuts and a new labour force development strategy are all contributing to a potential enhancement of productivity, flexibility and adaptability, which will be critical to ensure a remarkable quality of life to all Canadians in the Twenty-First Century.
Our initiatives have given results. Since 1984, Japan is the only country that has known a growth higher than Canada's. As regards jobs creation, Canada has been one of the most performing countries of the G-7. But our future also depends on our ability to train workers with more instruction and who are more and more skilled and specialized.
I know that my time is almost over, Mr. Speaker, but if you will allow me, I would just add that quality of life of Quebecers and Canadians is not only a question of exclusive competence or a question of jurisdiction. Quality of life is everyone's concern and it is the responsibility of everyone without exception.
As you know, my Francophone Liberal friends of Quebec talk about the problem of Constitution which has to be solved as soon as possible. They talk about unity, national consensus, but they have signed the repatriation in 1982 without Quebec, a mistake which we have been trying to rectify since then.
The Liberal strategy, Mr. Speaker, must have something machiavellian because the party of the hon. member for Beausejour has adopted this weekend in Sherbrooke a constitutional position copied from Meech Lake Accord.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, because I know that my time is almost over, our mission is clear. We are going to continue to work so that the Canadians can continue to be able to benefit from a competitive economy. We have never changed our goals since 1984 and we will not change them in the future. The Speech from the Throne shows that we are determined to reinforce the Canadian unity and our prosperity because both are linked.
By taking maximum advantage of the individuals and the richest education systems in the world, we will be able to compete with any country. The sustainable prosperity that will result will ensure the unity of our country for the benefit of all Quebecers and of the entire Canada.
